detailed_results.question: What are the possible causes if wireless devices cannot connect to the network?
detailed_results.expected: Possible causes include: WiFi is turned off on the router, incorrect wireless password entered, MAC Filtering blocking the device, incompatible wireless standard, or router needs to be restarted.
detailed_results.generated:
Possible causes include:  
1. Password mismatch – the Network Security Key is case-sensitive, so an incorrect or mistyped password will prevent authentication.  
2. Wrong SSID (wireless name) – if you’re trying to join a network name that doesn’t exactly match your router’s SSID, you won’t connect.  
3. Hidden SSID – if the router is set to “hide” its network name, devices won’t see it unless you manually enter the SSID.  
4. Incorrect region/country setting on the router – some regulatory domains disable certain channels or frequencies.  
5. Weak signal strength – with only 1–3 bars, the link may be too poor to establish or maintain a connection.  
6. Channel interference – if your router is on a crowded channel, try switching to channel 1, 6, or 11 to reduce overlap with nearby networks.  
7. Client-side timeouts or OS errors – Windows (or another OS) may report “Unable to connect,” “Cannot join this network,” or “Taking longer than usual to connect” if it can’t complete authentication or association.

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons Bandwidth Control may not seem to be working:

1. IP‐address mismatch  
   • Your rules are keyed off specific IPs but the PCs are on DHCP and may get different addresses.  
   • Solution: either give each machine a static IP or set up DHCP address reservation so the router can always match the rule to the correct host.

2. Global uplink/downlink values set incorrectly  
   • In the router’s Bandwidth Control page you must enter your actual WAN upload and download rates (typically a bit lower than your ISP-advertised speed).  
   • If those “total” values are wrong, the router can’t carve up bandwidth as you intended.

3. Sum of individual limits exceeds the real link speed  
   • If you assign limits that together are greater than your actual line rate, the router can’t enforce them.  
   • Make sure the sum of all “max” values ≤ your real WAN up/down speed.

4. Traffic bypassing the router  
   • VPN tunnels, another downstream switch/router, or modem-in-bridge mode can let traffic flow around the Bandwidth Control engine.  
   • Any device upstream of the router that isn’t under its control will break your shaping rules.

5. QoS/traffic-shaping engine disabled  
   • Some routers require you to explicitly turn on their QoS or traffic-shaping module in order for Bandwidth Control rules to be applied.  

If you check all of the above—static/reserved IPs, correct total link rates, sensible per-host limits, and ensure all traffic passes through the router’s QoS engine—Bandwidth Control should then work as expected.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?
detailed_results.expected: IP & MAC Binding (ARP) prevents ARP spoofing and ARP attacks by binding specific IP addresses to specific MAC addresses, ensuring only authorized devices can use those IP addresses on the network.
detailed_results.generated: The IP & MAC Binding feature lets you create a fixed (static) association between a device’s IP address and its MAC address in the router’s ARP table.  By doing so, any packet claiming to be from that IP but coming from a different MAC will be dropped.  This stops attackers from poisoning the ARP cache (ARP spoofing/ARP‐based attacks) and ensures that only the one, preapproved NIC can ever use that IP on your network.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control and MAC Filtering are both ways to keep unwanted devices off your LAN or WLAN, but they work at slightly different levels and offer different degrees of flexibility:

1. MAC Filtering  
  • Operates strictly on the link-layer address (the client’s 48-bit MAC).  
  • You build a simple table of “allowed” MACs (or sometimes “denied” MACs), and the AP or switch drops frames from any MAC not on that list.  
  • Typically used only on wireless radios, and offers no scheduling, grouping, or other criteria beyond “is this MAC in the list?”

2. Access Control  
  • A broader feature set that can cover both wired and wireless ports.  
  • Lets you maintain a whitelist (allowed devices) or blacklist (blocked devices) of clients—often still keyed by MAC, but sometimes by username, VLAN tag, time-of-day, etc.  
  • May pull an entry straight from your “Devices Online” view (so you don’t have to type in a long MAC by hand) and lets you annotate each entry (e.g. “Bob’s laptop,” “Guest phone”).  
  • Can be used to enforce policies (e.g. guests go to the VLAN 20 guest network, staff go to VLAN 10), schedule access windows, integrate with RADIUS, and more.

In short, MAC Filtering is a very basic form of Access Control that only matches a MAC address list on a wireless interface. True Access Control adds black-vs-white-list logic, works on both wired and wireless ports, and often ties into higher-level policy and authentication services.

Here’s the typical workflow for sharing a USB disk over your network so that any PC (or other SMB/FTP client) can browse it:

1. Physically attach the USB drive  
   • Plug your USB storage into the router’s USB port (or via a short USB cable).  
   • Wait until the USB LED on the router turns solid.

2. Enable “Local Storage Sharing” in the router’s web interface  
   • Log in to your router’s admin pages (usually by pointing a browser at 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1).  
   • Go to USB Settings → Local Storage Sharing (or Storage Sharing).  
   • Turn on the share, create any user-level permissions you want, and apply/save.

3. Access the share from a client on your LAN  
   – SMB (Windows/Mac/Linux file share)  
     • In Windows Explorer, enter \\<router-IP>\ (e.g. \\192.168.0.1\)  
     • In macOS Finder, choose “Go→Connect to Server…” and type smb://<router-IP>/  
   – FTP (if your router supports an FTP service)  
     • In a browser or FTP client, point to ftp://<router-IP>/  

4. (Optional) Map it as a network drive  
   • In Windows: right-click “This PC” → “Map network drive…” → enter \\<router-IP>\<share-name>  
   • In macOS: after connecting via smb://, drag the share’s icon in Finder to your sidebar.

That’s it—once “Local Storage Sharing” is on, any authorized machine on your LAN (and, if you open the right ports, even over the Internet) can browse the USB drive just as if it were a shared folder on your PC.

detailed_results.question: What are the possible causes if wireless devices cannot connect to the network?
detailed_results.expected: Possible causes include: WiFi is turned off on the router, incorrect wireless password entered, MAC Filtering blocking the device, incompatible wireless standard, or router needs to be restarted.
detailed_results.generated:
Possible causes include:  
1. Weak or unreliable signal  
   - Your device is too far from the router (only 1–3 bars).  
   - Physical obstacles or interference (walls, metal objects, other electronics).  

2. Radio-frequency interference  
   - Nearby Wi-Fi networks on the same channel.  
   - Other devices (microwaves, cordless phones) operating on 2.4 GHz.  
   → Try switching your router’s channel to 1, 6 or 11.  

3. Incorrect wireless settings on the router  
   - Wrong SSID (network name) or you’ve accidentally hidden the SSID.  
   - Region/country setting mismatched (some channels disabled in certain regions).  

4. Driver or software issues on the client  
   - The wireless adapter driver is missing, outdated or corrupt.  
   - On Windows the Wi-Fi radio may be turned off or “blocked” by airplane mode.  
   - On XP the built-in Wireless Configuration service might be disabled or you’re running a third-party wireless utility that conflicts with it.  

5. Authentication or encryption mismatch  
   - You’re entering the wrong wireless password or using the wrong security type (WEP/WPA/WPA2).  

6. Router‐side restrictions  
   - MAC-address filtering or access control enabled on the router limiting which devices can join.  

If you can still see the network but can’t join, try your OS’s built-in Troubleshooter (e.g. Windows 7 “Troubleshoot” link) or check for any third-party Wi-Fi management software that might be blocking the connection.

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons you might turn on Bandwidth Control in your router’s GUI and still not see it working as you expected:

1. IP‐address mismatches  
   • You didn’t give each client a static IP (or reserve its DHCP address), so its address keeps changing and no rule ever “hits.”  
   • You entered the wrong IP or range in your control rule (typo, wrong subnet mask, etc.).  

2. Total‐bandwidth values are wrong  
   • You must enter the actual upstream/downstream rates your ISP is providing (in Kbps). If you overstate them, the router can’t shape properly.  
   • Mixing up Kbps vs. Mbps (e.g. typing “8 Mbps” as “8000” when the router expects “8192”).  

3. Bandwidth Control wasn’t fully enabled/saved  
   • After you type in the total bandwidth, you need to click “Save” or “Apply” on the Bandwidth Control page.  
   • You also have to toggle the overall feature “On” before individual rules take effect.  

4. Rule conflicts or ordering issues  
   • Overlapping IP ranges or duplicate rules can negate each other.  
   • If you have a “minimum guaranteed” rule but no corresponding maximum, bursty clients may still grab more bandwidth.  

5. Encrypted or tunneled traffic  
   • VPNs, SSH tunnels or some P2P protocols can bypass application-level QoS, making per-port or per-protocol shaping ineffective.  
   • The router can only throttle traffic it sees; fully encrypted streams sometimes escape its classification.  

6. Upstream shaping limitations  
   • Some home routers can’t truly shape upstream traffic (they can only police it based on what they themselves generate). If your ISP enforces the line rate strictly, you may not be able to limit uploads any further.  

If you check those points—static IP/reservations, correct total‐bandwidth entries, saved/enabled settings, non-overlapping rules, and whether the traffic is visible to the router—you’ll usually find what’s preventing the limits from taking effect.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?
detailed_results.expected: IP & MAC Binding (ARP) prevents ARP spoofing and ARP attacks by binding specific IP addresses to specific MAC addresses, ensuring only authorized devices can use those IP addresses on the network.
detailed_results.generated: The IP & MAC Binding feature ties (binds) a device’s IP address to its unique MAC address so that only the one “known” NIC can ever use that IP on your LAN.  By doing so the router can reject ARP replies or requests that claim a legitimate IP but come from an un-recognized MAC, effectively blocking ARP spoofing and related man-in-the-middle attacks.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control and MAC Filtering both use the MAC (hardware) address of a client to decide whether it may join your network, but they differ in scope and flexibility:

1. MAC Filtering  
   • Applies only to wireless clients.  
   • You build a single list of allowed (or blocked) MAC addresses on the WLAN SSID.  
   • Any device whose MAC is not on the “allow” list (or is on the “deny” list) will be refused association to the wireless network.  

2. Access Control  
   • Works for both wired and wireless clients.  
   • Lets you maintain separate blacklists (devices to block) and whitelists (devices to allow).  
   • Enforces those lists network-wide, not just on the wireless SSID.  

In short, MAC Filtering is a wireless-only allow/deny list. Access Control is a broader feature—you can centrally blacklist or whitelist devices by MAC on your entire LAN (wired and wireless).

   – Router is set to the wrong region, limiting available channels

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons why the Bandwidth Control feature may not behave the way you expect:  

1. You haven’t fixed each PC’s LAN IP  
   •  By default most routers hand out addresses via DHCP. If one of your PCs gets a new IP when its lease renews the old rule no longer matches, so it won’t be rate-limited or guaranteed any bandwidth.  
   •  Always either set a static IP on the machine itself or use Address Reservation (DHCP Binding) in the router so that the IP never changes.  

2. Your “Total Up/Down Bandwidth” numbers don’t match your real line speed  
   •  If you enter higher upstream/downstream rates than your ISP actually delivers, the router can’t shape traffic to something faster than the line.  
   •  If you enter significantly lower rates, you’ll be needlessly throttling everything.  
   →  Always run a speed test, then enter as your “Total” about 90–95% of the measured values (in Kbps).  

3. You picked the wrong “Line Type”  
   •  The router asks for DSL/Cable/etc. Picking the wrong one can confuse its driver for how to meter packets and apply your rules.  
   •  If in doubt, call your ISP to confirm which line type and encapsulation you’re on.  

4. Your IP-range or port-range rules overlap or don’t cover all ports  
   •  By default BC rules match port 1–65535. If you change that range on several rules and they overlap, the router may only honor the first match.  
   •  If you only shape TCP but your apps use UDP (or vice versa), you’ll see “unshaped” bursts.  

5. You’ve assigned more guaranteed (minimum) bandwidth than your total  
   •  If the sum of all of your Min-Bandwidth settings exceeds the Total Upstream or Downstream, the router can’t possibly satisfy every guarantee at once.  

6. Firmware bugs or hardware limitations  
   •  Make sure you’re running the latest official firmware for your exact router model—some early releases had BC quirks.  
   •  Very cheap or older routers may simply be unable to police high-speed links accurately under heavy load.  

If you check all of the above (static IPs or reservations, correct total rates, right line type, non-overlapping rules, and up-to-date firmware) your Bandwidth Control should start working as intended.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?
detailed_results.expected: IP & MAC Binding (ARP) prevents ARP spoofing and ARP attacks by binding specific IP addresses to specific MAC addresses, ensuring only authorized devices can use those IP addresses on the network.
detailed_results.generated: The IP & MAC Binding feature (also called ARP Binding) lets you tie a specific IP address to a specific MAC address.  By doing so, the router will only honor ARP requests for that IP if they come from the bound MAC.  Any device spoofing the IP with a different MAC is blocked, which effectively prevents ARP spoofing and related ARP-based attacks.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control is the router’s more general “allow or deny” mechanism for every device (whether it’s on your Wi-Fi or plugged in by cable).  You set it up in one of two modes:  
  •  Whitelist mode – only the devices you explicitly add may join your network.  
  •  Blacklist mode – every device may join except those you explicitly add.  

MAC Filtering, by contrast, is a simpler, wireless-only feature that uses just the MAC address of a client to decide if it may associate to your SSID.  In other words:  
  •  MAC Filtering = a wireless-only allow/deny list based purely on MAC addresses.  
  •  Access Control = a unified allow/deny list (blacklist or whitelist) that applies to both wired and wireless clients.

detailed_results.question: What are the possible causes if wireless devices cannot connect to the network?

Here are the most common reasons a wireless device can’t join a network. Depending on whether you can see your SSID at all or you see it but can’t authenticate, one or more of these will apply:

1. Device-side radio/driver issues  
   • The laptop’s or adapter’s wireless radio is turned off (hardware switch, function key or BIOS)  
   • The wireless adapter driver isn’t installed or has been disabled in Device Manager  
   • On XP, the Wireless Zero Configuration (or Windows WLAN AutoConfig) service is not set to Automatic or not running  
   • A third-party utility (e.g. manufacturer’s Wi-Fi manager) is conflicting with Windows’ built-in wireless service  

2. No networks or only other networks visible  
   • Your router’s WLAN is turned off (check the WLAN LED)  
   • Your device is out of range or the signal is too weak (move closer)  
   • The router’s SSID broadcast is hidden  
   • The router’s region/country setting doesn’t match your device’s setting  

3. You see your SSID but can’t connect  
   • Authentication failure – wrong wireless password (Network Security Key) or PIN  
   • Password/Key is case-sensitive or you’re entering a PIN when the network expects a passphrase  
   • You’ve exceeded the router’s maximum client count or MAC-filtering is enabled  

4. Environment and interference  
   • Wireless channel congestion – many nearby networks on the same channel (try channels 1, 6 or 11)  
   • Physical obstructions or electronic interference degrading signal quality  

5. Router configuration problems  
   • Mismatched wireless mode (e.g. router set to “n only,” client only supports “g”)  
   • Security mode mismatch (WPA vs. WPA2, mixed mode, etc.)  
   • SSID/password recently changed on the router but devices still using the old settings  

By working through these areas—device radio and driver, router radio and SSID settings, authentication parameters, and interference—you can usually pinpoint why a wireless device won’t join the network.

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons Bandwidth Control on a TP-Link modem/router appears to do nothing—usually it isn’t broken, it’s just mis-configured:

1. No fixed IP for the client  
   • If your PCs are getting dynamic DHCP leases, their addresses can change and your rules no longer match. Either give each machine a static LAN IP or use the router’s “Address Reservation” so that the IPs never shift.

2. Total bandwidth set incorrectly  
   • You must enter the actual upstream/downstream rates your ISP provides (in Kbps). If you over- or under-state those numbers the router can’t enforce your per-IP limits properly.

3. Wrong “Line Type” selected  
   • In Advanced → Bandwidth Control you must pick the correct DSL/PPPoE/ethernet type to match your WAN. If in doubt, ask your ISP.

4. Rules aren’t enabled or saved  
   • After you click Add … make sure the checkbox for that entry is ticked and you click OK (and Save) on the main Bandwidth Control page.

5. IP range or ports mis-specified  
   • If you enter the wrong single IP or an overlapping/wrong IP range, your target device won’t fall into the rule. Likewise, if you change the default port range or protocol, make sure it matches the traffic you actually want to limit.

6. Priority conflicts  
   • Lower numerical priority means “higher priority.” If two rules overlap, the one with the smaller priority number wins, which can look like your intended limit isn’t being applied.

Double-check each of the above in your Bandwidth Control settings—once your total link speed, line type, static IPs, and rules are all correct and enabled, per-IP limits will start working as expected.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?
detailed_results.expected: IP & MAC Binding (ARP) prevents ARP spoofing and ARP attacks by binding specific IP addresses to specific MAC addresses, ensuring only authorized devices can use those IP addresses on the network.
detailed_results.generated:
The IP & MAC Binding feature (sometimes called ARP Binding) is a security mechanism that locks each device’s IP address to its physical (MAC) address.  By doing so, it:

• Prevents ARP spoofing and other ARP-based attacks  
• Ensures that only the device with the approved MAC can use its assigned IP  
• Blocks any device that tries to use a bound IP with an unrecognized MAC  

In short, it protects your LAN by making sure IP↔MAC mappings stay legitimate.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control is a network‐level allow/block mechanism you configure under Advanced > Security that works on both your wired and your wireless LAN.  It lets you build either a “blacklist” of devices you always block or a “whitelist” of devices you alone permit.  When Access Control is turned on, any device whose MAC (or IP & MAC, depending on the router) appears in your block list can’t use the network, and any device in your allow list is the only one that can.

MAC Filtering, by contrast, is strictly a wireless-only feature (found under Advanced > Wireless > MAC Filtering) that lets you block or permit individual Wi-Fi clients by their MAC address.  

In practice the differences are:

• Scope  
  – Access Control applies to both wired and wireless interfaces.  
  – MAC Filtering applies only to Wi-Fi clients.  

• List organization  
  – Access Control explicitly separates a blacklist (block list) from a whitelist (allow list).  
  – MAC Filtering usually just gives you a single list and lets you choose whether it’s being used to block or to allow.  

• Typical use cases  
  – Use Access Control when you need a single policy for every device on your LAN, regardless of how it’s connected.  
  – Use MAC Filtering when you only care about limiting which clients can associate to your Wi-Fi.

detailed_results.question: What should you do if you cannot access the router's web interface?
detailed_results.expected: Check that your device is connected to the router (wired or wireless), verify you're using the correct address (tplinkmodem.net or 192.168.1.1), try a different web browser, and ensure no firewall is blocking access.
detailed_results.generated:
If you can’t reach the router’s web-based setup page, try the following in order:

1. Check physical connections  
   • Make sure the router is powered on and the Ethernet cable between your PC and the router LAN port is firmly seated.  
   • Verify the corresponding LAN LED on the router lights up.

2. Verify your PC’s TCP/IP settings  
   • Set your computer’s IPv4 to obtain an IP address automatically (via DHCP).  
   • Set it to obtain the DNS server address automatically as well.

3. Confirm the address you’re using to log in  
   • Use the correct default gateway (usually 192.168.1.1 or whatever is printed on your router label).  
   • Make sure you’re typing the URL/IP into your browser’s address bar (not a search box).

4. Check your PC’s Internet Options (Windows example)  
   a. Go to Control Panel > Network and Internet > View network status and tasks  
   b. Click Internet Options (bottom left)  
   c. On the Connections tab, select “Never dial a connection”  
   d. Click LAN Settings and make sure all three checkboxes are UNchecked; click OK  
   e. On the Advanced tab, click “Restore advanced settings,” then OK

5. Try a different browser or PC  
   • Sometimes browser extensions or cached pages interfere.  
   • If possible, plug another computer into the router and attempt to log in.

6. Reset the router to factory defaults  
   • With the router powered on, press and hold the WPS/RESET button on the back for about 8 seconds, until all LEDs blink on, then release.  
   • You’ll need to reconfigure the router from scratch afterward (use the Quick Setup Wizard).

If after all that you still can’t log in, contact your router’s technical support for further assistance.

detailed_results.question: How do you recover access if you forgot the router's login password?
detailed_results.expected: If you forgot the password, you must reset the router to factory defaults by pressing and holding the RESET button for 8 seconds. After reset, you'll need to set a new password when accessing the router.
detailed_results.generated:
If you can’t remember the user-name or password you set for the web interface, the only way back in is to reset the modem-router to its factory defaults. Here’s how:

1. Make sure the router is powered on.  
2. Press and hold the WPS/RESET button on the back for about 8 seconds (until all LEDs briefly go out and then back on).  
3. Release the button and wait for the router to reboot (this can take a minute or two).  

After the reset, the router’s admin name and password revert to the factory defaults (check the label on the bottom or back of the unit for the default user name, password/PIN and the login URL—often http://tplinkmodem.net or 192.168.1.1). 

Once you’re back in, you’ll need to run the Quick Setup or re-enter your ISP details and Wi-Fi settings, and then set a new admin password under Advanced > System Tools > Administration (or similar).

detailed_results.question: What does it mean if the ADSL LED is not lit on the router?
detailed_results.expected: If the ADSL LED is not lit, it means there's no DSL connection. Check that the DSL cable is properly connected to the phone jack or splitter, verify the cable is not damaged, and confirm DSL service is active with your ISP.
detailed_results.generated:
If the ADSL LED is off it means the modem-router has failed to synchronize with your DSL line. In other words, it isn’t detecting a usable ADSL signal. 

What to do next (see Note 1 in the manual):  
1. Verify that your phone cable is correctly plugged into the ADSL port and into a working jack (and that any splitter/filters are installed properly).  
2. If cabling is correct but the LED remains off, contact your ISP to confirm that your ADSL service is active and that there are no line issues on their end.

detailed_results.question: What are the possible causes if wireless devices cannot connect to the network?
detailed_results.expected: Possible causes include: WiFi is turned off on the router, incorrect wireless password entered, MAC Filtering blocking the device, incompatible wireless standard, or router needs to be restarted.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons a wireless client can’t join your network. Depending on whether the network “doesn’t even show up” or you can see it but “can’t connect,” some of these will apply more than others.

1. Wireless radio or adapter is off/disabled  
   • On many laptops there’s a hardware switch or Fn-key combo; on desktops the PCI/USB adapter may be disabled in Device Manager.  
   • Driver not installed or corrupted.

2. SSID issues  
   • Your router’s SSID is hidden.  
   • You’ve selected the wrong SSID or keyed it in incorrectly.  
   • Region/Country setting on the router is wrong, so the AP isn’t broadcasting on legal channels.

3. Authentication (password/PIN) problems  
   • You’re using the wrong Wireless Password/Network Security Key (it’s case-sensitive).  
   • You’ve tried to use the device’s “PIN” instead of the actual wireless passphrase.  
   • The router’s WPA/WPA2 settings don’t match what the client expects.

4. Signal strength or interference  
   • You’re simply too far from the AP (1–3 bars is marginal).  
   • Co-channel or adjacent-channel interference—try switching your router to channel 1, 6 or 11.

5. Software/service conflicts (Windows)  
   • On XP the Wireless Zero Configuration service is stopped or set to manual.  
   • You’re running a third-party wireless utility (e.g. TP-Link Utility) that conflicts with Windows’ own.  
   • On Win7 “No connections are available” can mean the built-in wireless service is disabled—running the Windows troubleshooter sometimes fixes it.

6. Adapter driver problems  
   • The client’s wireless driver is out of date or corrupted; reinstall or update it.  
   • In some cases you may need to uninstall the old driver, reboot, then let Windows detect and install a fresh copy.

If you’ve checked all the above and still can’t join, try the built-in Troubleshoot function in Windows, or reset your router to factory defaults and reconfigure its SSID/security from scratch.

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons you may find that Bandwidth Control isn’t doing what you expect:

1. Total Up/Down values are wrong  
   – You must enter your ISP-guaranteed line rate in Kbps (1 Mbps = 1024 Kbps). If you over- or under-estimate, the router can’t police traffic correctly.  

2. Devices aren’t on a fixed (or reserved) IP  
   – If your PCs are getting DHCP addresses and those change, the rules you set no longer match. Either give each target machine a static LAN IP or use Address Reservation.  

3. Rule entries aren’t enabled, overlap, or conflict  
   – After you “Add” each rule, you must check its “Enable” box.  
   – Make sure your IP ranges don’t overlap or you may end up with no effective control (or unintended sharing).  
   – Double-check you’re not accidentally creating two rules for the same IP with contradictory settings.  

4. Protocol or port filters are too narrow  
   – By default the port range is 1–65535 and protocol is TCP&UDP. If you change either, you may miss some of the traffic (e.g. many games and streaming services use UDP).  

5. Wrong Line Type selected  
   – Under Advanced > Bandwidth Control you must pick the correct WAN/DSL type (ADSL2+, VDSL, Ethernet WAN, etc.) to match your ISP’s service. The router needs that to apply QoS.  

If you’ve verified all of the above and it still “doesn’t work,” try rebooting the router after saving, make sure you’re on the latest firmware, and re-check all your entries.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?
detailed_results.expected: IP & MAC Binding (ARP) prevents ARP spoofing and ARP attacks by binding specific IP addresses to specific MAC addresses, ensuring only authorized devices can use those IP addresses on the network.
detailed_results.generated: The IP & MAC Binding feature (also called ARP Binding) is used to tie each device’s IP address to its unique MAC address.  By doing so the router will refuse any ARP requests or traffic claiming an IP in the binding list unless it comes from the matching MAC, effectively preventing ARP spoofing and related man-in-the-middle attacks.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control and MAC Filtering both let you use a device’s MAC address to decide who gets on your network, but they differ in scope and where/how you configure them:

1. What is Access Control?  
   • A system-level “blacklist/whitelist” for both wired and wireless clients.  
   • You can turn it on under Advanced > Security > Access Control.  
   • You choose whether you’re running in “Blacklist” mode (everything is allowed except devices you block) or “Whitelist” mode (nothing is allowed except devices you explicitly add).  
   • You can pick devices straight out of your current online‐device table, click “Block” or “Allow,” and they’ll be added to the appropriate list.

2. What is MAC Filtering?  
   • A wireless-only feature that blocks or permits devices based on MAC address.  
   • You configure it under Advanced > Wireless > MAC Filtering.  
   • In “Block” mode you stop selected wireless MACs from connecting; in “Allow” mode only listed MACs can join.  
   • You typically have to type or paste each MAC and give it a description before enabling it.

Key differences at a glance:  
• Scope: Access Control works on both wired and wireless ports; MAC Filtering applies only to Wi-Fi.  
• Setup Location: Access Control lives in Security settings; MAC Filtering lives in Wireless settings.  
• Workflow: Access Control can pull devices directly from your online-devices list; MAC Filtering usually requires manually entering each MAC.

    •  Either use the default “admin” or create a new user.  
    •  Click Save.  
    •  Turn on “Enable Authentication” (so only your account can log in).  

3.  Enable FTP over the Internet  
    •  Still in Advanced → USB Settings → Sharing Access (or “Remote Access via FTP”),  
    •  Check “Enable FTP (via Internet)”, then Save.  

4.  Connect from anywhere  
    •  In any FTP client or even a web browser / Windows Explorer address bar, point to:  
       ftp://tplinkmodem.net  
       (or ftp://<your-router’s-WAN-IP>)  
    •  Log in with the username/password you set.  
    •  You’ll now see your USB folders and files just as if you were on your home LAN.

detailed_results.question: How do you set up the router using Quick Setup Wizard?
detailed_results.expected: Log in to the router interface, click Quick Setup, select your ISP from the dropdown list, then follow the on-screen instructions to complete the setup.
detailed_results.generated:
Here’s how to get your TP-Link modem-router up and running in just a few minutes using the Quick Setup Wizard:

1. Physical & network connection  
   • Make sure the modem-router is powered on.  
   • If you have a built-in DSL port, connect your phone line to the modem’s DSL port.  
     – If you already have a separate modem or your ISP delivers Internet via an Ethernet jack in the wall, plug that Ethernet cable into the modem-router’s WAN (Internet) port instead.  
   • Connect your PC (or tablet) to the modem-router by Ethernet cable or via the default Wi-Fi network printed on the label.

2. Log in to the web interface  
   • Open a browser and go to http://tplinkmodem.net  
   • Log in with the router password you created when you first powered it up (or the default admin password if this is your first time).

3. Launch Quick Setup  
   • In the left-hand menu, click “Quick Setup.”  
   • Click Next.

4. Select your Internet (WAN) connection type  
   • From the ISP dropdown list pick your provider if it’s listed.  
   • If it isn’t listed, choose “Other.”  
   • Click Next.

5. Enter your ISP details  
   Depending on the connection type your ISP gave you, you may need to enter:  
   • PPPoE username & password (for most DSL plans)  
   • Static IP, subnet mask, gateway & DNS servers (for static‐IP plans)  
   • Or simply leave it on Dynamic IP (DHCP) if that’s how your ISP works.  
   Click Next when done.

6. (Optional) Change wireless settings  
   • You’ll be prompted to set your Wireless Network Name (SSID) and a Wireless Password.  
   • If you change these from the defaults, you’ll need to reconnect all your Wi-Fi devices using the new SSID/password.  
   Click Next.

7. Review & Finish  
   • The wizard will show you a summary of the settings you entered.  
   • Click “Save” or “Finish.”  
   • The router will reboot to apply the new settings.

8. Reconnect your devices  
   • After the reboot, verify you have Internet access.  
   • If you changed the SSID/password, search for the new wireless network on your devices and connect using the new password.

That’s it—the Quick Setup Wizard walks you through choosing your ISP, entering any login or IP details, and securing your Wi-Fi in just a few screens.

Here are the most common causes for “I’ve set up bandwidth control but it doesn’t seem to be working”:

1. Mis-matched interface or direction  
   – On most SOHO routers you shape “Upload” on the WAN port and “Download” on the LAN side. If you apply the rule to the wrong interface (e.g. put your downstream limits on the WAN interface) nothing gets enforced.  

2. IP/MAC binding doesn’t stick  
   – Your rules are tied to a specific static IP (or MAC), but your client is getting a different DHCP address (or spoofing MAC). If the address in your BC rule doesn’t match the host’s actual address, the router never sees a rule to apply.  

3. Guaranteed bandwidths sum to more than your pipe  
   – If you assign minimums that add up to more than your actual ISP link, the router can’t honor every guarantee simultaneously, so some hosts end up getting full blast anyway.  

4. Encrypted/VPN or tunneled traffic  
   – Once you wrap everything in a single VPN or SSH tunnel, the router only sees one “big” flow. It can’t distinguish the individual streams inside, so your per-PC or per-port rules simply don’t apply.  

5. Certain protocols are unshaped  
   – ICMP, broadcast, multicast, DHCP, some VoIP or P2P UDP ports may bypass or be very coarsely queued by the router. If your user is on one of those, it may look like BC is completely off.  

6. Rule priority or absence of a catch-all  
   – Most routers process bandwidth rules top-down. If you haven’t created a default low-priority rule at the bottom, “unmatched” traffic will roam free at full speed. Also make sure your max-bandwidth rules don’t get overridden by higher-priority minimum-bandwidth rules.  

7. Firmware bugs or limitations  
   – Especially on cheap routers, the QoS/BC engine can be buggy or only approximate. If you suspect this, check for firmware updates or try a third-party build (DD-WRT, OpenWrt, Tomato, etc.) that has a more robust traffic-shaping implementation.

If you systematically check each of these points—interface, IP/MAC binding, sum of guarantees, encryption, protocol coverage, rule ordering and firmware quality—you’ll almost always uncover why the limits aren’t behaving as you expected.

The IP & MAC Binding feature is there to lock a given IP address to a single, known MAC address so that:  
• Only that specific device ever uses that IP on your LAN  
• ARP spoofing or poisoning attacks (where a rogue MAC claims another device’s IP) are prevented  
• IP-conflicts and unauthorized access are effectively blocked  

In short, by binding IPs to MACs you ensure each address can only be claimed by its legitimate NIC, greatly improving local-network security.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control is the router’s built-in mechanism for permitting or denying devices on both your wired and your wireless LAN based on a set of administrator-defined rules.  In most SOHO routers it lets you maintain “allow” and “deny” lists for client devices (and often schedule when they may or may not connect), regardless of whether they arrive over Ethernet or Wi-Fi.  

By contrast, MAC Filtering is a much narrower feature that only looks at a device’s hardware (MAC) address and only on the wireless side.  You build an approved (or blocked) list of MAC addresses, and any wireless client whose MAC does not appear on that list is refused association to the SSID.  

In short:  
•  MAC Filtering = wireless-only, filters solely by MAC address  
•  Access Control = both wired & wireless, can filter by MAC and/or other criteria (time schedules, port, SSID, etc.)

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?

1. You never actually added any rules.

2. Your rule’s IP address (or range) doesn’t match the client you’re testing.  
   – If you’re using DHCP and the client’s address changed, the router never applies your rule.  
   – Solution: give each client a static IP or set up Address Reservation, then re-create the rule.

3. You entered the wrong total upstream/downstream values.  
   – Make sure you convert correctly: 1 Mbps = 1024 Kbps. If you over-report your actual ISP speed the router won’t need to shape, and if you under-report it you’ll throttle everything unintentionally.

4. You picked the wrong “line type” (DSL vs. cable, etc.).  
   – The shaping engine uses different defaults for each line type. If in doubt, ask your ISP which one you should choose.

5. You changed the default port-range or protocol in a way that excludes your traffic.  
   – By default it’s TCP/UDP ports 1–65535. If you narrow that down you may accidentally leave out whatever ports your application is using.

Bonus checks if you’re still stuck:  
• Save and reboot the modem-router after making your changes.  
• Make sure you’re running the latest firmware (older releases sometimes have QoS bugs).  
• Test with a simple download/upload (e.g. an FTP transfer) so you can easily measure before/after speeds.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?

By doing so, the router will only honor ARP requests for that IP when they come from the bound MAC.  Any device claiming the same IP but with a different (unbound) MAC will be denied access.  This effectively blocks ARP spoofing/poisoning attacks and helps keep your LAN more secure.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?

  • or a Blacklist (everybody except these devices gets on)  

MAC Filtering, by contrast, is that same idea applied only to your wireless interface and using only the device’s MAC address as its identifier.  In other words:  
  1. MAC Filtering = Wi-Fi only, permit or deny based strictly on MAC  
  2. Access Control = both wired and wireless, permit or deny based on a maintained allow/deny list of devices

detailed_results.question: What are the possible causes if wireless devices cannot connect to the network?

Here are the most common reasons a wireless‐capable device may see your network but be unable to join it.  Depending on your exact model and OS, you may need to check one or more of these:

1.  Wireless radio is turned off  
    • On the router – the WLAN/Wi-Fi LED is off or the wireless function has been disabled in the router’s settings.  
    • On the client – laptop hardware switch or function-key radio switch is off, or the adapter has been disabled in your OS.

2.  Out of range or very weak signal  
    • Your device shows only 1–3 bars. Move closer to the router or remove obstacles.  
    • Heavy interference from neighboring networks—try setting your router to channel 1, 6, or 11.

3.  Driver or service issues on the client  
    • Wireless-adapter driver is missing, corrupted or out of date.  
    • The OS wireless‐network service (e.g. WLAN AutoConfig in Windows) is not running.

4.  SSID or region settings mismatch  
    • You’ve entered the wrong network name (SSID).  
    • The router’s SSID broadcast is hidden.  
    • The router’s Region/Country setting doesn’t match your locale and prevents your client from using the chosen channel.

5.  Authentication (password/PIN) problems  
    • You’re using the router’s PIN instead of the Wi-Fi password (or vice versa).  
    • The network security key (WEP/WPA/WPA2 passphrase) was mistyped—remember it is case-sensitive.  
    • Your device’s security type (WPA vs. WPA2, TKIP vs. AES) doesn’t match the router’s.

6.  Access‐control restrictions on the router  
    • MAC-filtering is enabled and your client’s MAC address isn’t on the allow list.  
    • You’ve reached the router’s maximum number of DHCP/connected clients.

If you’ve checked all of the above and still cannot connect, reboot both router and client, verify you haven’t accidentally enabled any advanced restrictions (e.g. RADIUS, guest isolation), and then retry.

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons you’ll see “Bandwidth Control” seemingly doing nothing on a TP-Link modem/router:

1. Bandwidth Control isn’t actually turned on  
   • After logging into http://tplinkmodem.net, make sure you’ve ticked “Enable Bandwidth Control” and clicked Save.  

2. Wrong line type or total bandwidth values  
   • If you pick the wrong line type (DSL vs. Cable) the router won’t shape traffic correctly – check with your ISP.  
   • You must enter your real upstream/downstream numbers (e.g. if your ISP gives you 1 Mbps up, enter 1024 Kbps).  

3. Rules don’t match your PCs’ IPs  
   • If your machines get their IPs by DHCP, they may change and fall outside your “IP Range” rules.  
   • Solution: assign each computer a static IP or use the router’s address-reservation feature, then build your rules against that IP (or IP range).  

4. Protocol or port settings exclude some traffic  
   • By default the port range is 1–65535 and “ALL” protocols. If you accidentally limit to TCP only (or to a narrow port range), UDP or other ports won’t be shaped.  

5. Priority or sum of allocations is off  
   • Lower “Priority” values get served first. If you give one PC a very high priority, it may grab all the bandwidth.  
   • If the sum of all your per-PC upstream/downstream limits exceeds the total you entered, the router can’t honor every rule.  

6. Individual rules aren’t enabled or haven’t been saved  
   • After you “Add” a rule you still have to check the “Enable” box for that entry and click OK/Save.  

Bottom line: Bandwidth Control only works if (a) the feature is enabled, (b) the total line speed is entered correctly, (c) you’ve reserved or statically assigned IPs, and (d) your per-IP rules (protocol, ports, priorities and rates) are valid and enabled. If any one of those steps is missed or mis-configured, the router will simply pass traffic unconstrained.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?
detailed_results.expected: IP & MAC Binding (ARP) prevents ARP spoofing and ARP attacks by binding specific IP addresses to specific MAC addresses, ensuring only authorized devices can use those IP addresses on the network.
detailed_results.generated: The IP & MAC Binding feature (also known as ARP Binding) lets you lock a specific IP address to a single, known MAC address.  By doing so, the router will refuse ARP requests from any device that claims that IP but doesn’t present the matching MAC.  This effectively blocks ARP spoofing and other ARP-based attacks, since no one can hijack (or “poison”) the ARP table by pretending to be another IP on your LAN.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control is the router’s “master” allow-or-block list for any client—wired or wireless—where you explicitly put devices on a whitelist (allowed) or a blacklist (blocked).  You can point to the same MAC or IP addresses you see in your online-devices table and tell the router “never let these in” or “only let these in,” regardless of how they connect.

By contrast, MAC Filtering is a simpler, wireless-only feature.  It looks only at a device’s MAC address and either admits or rejects it from the Wi-Fi based on the list you build under Wireless > MAC Filtering.  In short:

• MAC Filtering  
 – Wireless only  
 – Purely MAC-address based  
 – Either block or allow on the wireless side  

• Access Control  
 – Both wired and wireless  
 – Uses a whitelist/blacklist model  
 – Can combine MAC (and even IP via IP & MAC Binding)  
 – Applies globally to all network ports and SSIDs

detailed_results.question: What are the possible causes if wireless devices cannot connect to the network?

Here are the most common reasons a wireless client can’t see or join your Wi-Fi network, grouped by symptom:

1. You see no networks at all  
   • The PC’s wireless radio is turned off or “airplane mode” is on  
   • The wireless adapter isn’t installed, enabled or its driver is missing/out of date  
   • On Windows XP the Wireless Zero Configuration service is stopped or you have another utility running  

2. You see other networks but not yours  
   • Your router’s WLAN radio/LED is off  
   • You’re out of range (signal too weak—move closer)  
   • You’ve hidden (disabled SSID broadcast) or mistyped your SSID  
   • You’ve set the wrong Region/Country or non-standard channel  

3. You see your SSID but can’t join  
   • Authentication failure – wrong network key/password (case-sensitive)  
   • Confusing the router’s PIN (WPS PIN) with the WPA/WPA2 passphrase  
   • Channel congestion or interference (try channels 1, 6 or 11)  
   • The router’s security (MAC filtering, access control) is blocking the device  

4. Connection attempts time out or stall  
   • Signal strength is very low (only 1–3 bars)  
   • Wireless adapter driver needs reinstalling or updating  
   • The router is overloaded or needs a reboot

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons you’ll see “Bandwidth Control” rules not having any effect on your traffic.  In almost every case it comes down to a mis-configuration in one of the steps:

1. Bandwidth Control isn’t actually turned on  
   • You must ENABLE the feature on Advanced → Bandwidth Control before your rules will apply.  
   • If you skip that checkbox, none of your per-IP or per-range rules do anything.

2. The total uplink/downlink values are wrong  
   • On the same page you enter your ISP’s total Upstream and Downstream bandwidth (in Kbps).  
   • If you enter a value that’s too low or too high, every rule will scale off the wrong base and look “ineffective.”  
   • Double-check with your ISP whether they quote in Mbps or Kbps, and convert 1 Mbps = 1024 Kbps.

3. Wrong line type selected (DSL vs. Cable)  
   • The router needs to know whether it’s shaping on a DSL or a cable/fiber link.  
   • If you pick the wrong one, your throttles won’t line up with the real transmit queue.

4. IP addresses in your rules don’t match the clients  
   • You must either give each PC a static IP or reserve its DHCP address in the router.  
   • If a client’s IP changes, your rule never sees its traffic and can’t shape it.

5. Your IP-range or port-range entries are off  
   • A single-IP rule only applies to exactly that address; a range only applies to those in its span.  
   • Make sure you didn’t accidentally type 192.168.1.1–192.168.1.10 when you really meant .101–.110.  
   • In almost all basic setups you can leave the Port Range at 1–65535 and Protocol on “All.”

6. Conflicting or overlapping rules  
   • If two rules both match the same IP or traffic, the router may use the higher-priority one or ignore one altogether.  
   • Check your Priority field (lower number = higher priority) and make sure no two rules collide.

7. Guest-network shaping depends on the main control  
   • If you enabled guest-network bandwidth control but forgot to turn on the global Bandwidth Control, the guest limits won’t apply.

8. Firmware bugs or old firmware  
   • Very occasionally you’ll run into a software bug that keeps Bandwidth Control from working.  
   • Check for and install the latest router firmware before digging too deep.

If you’ve walked through every step in Advanced → Bandwidth Control—set the global uplink/downlink, enabled the feature, created correct rules tied to static/reserved IPs, chosen the right line type, and avoided overlaps—and it still does nothing, you may need to contact TP-Link support or try a firmware update.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?
detailed_results.expected: IP & MAC Binding (ARP) prevents ARP spoofing and ARP attacks by binding specific IP addresses to specific MAC addresses, ensuring only authorized devices can use those IP addresses on the network.
detailed_results.generated: The IP & MAC Binding feature (also called ARP Binding) lets you lock down each LAN IP address to a specific physical device (MAC address).  By doing so, the router will only honor ARP requests for that IP if they come from the bound MAC—and will drop any ARP packets that claim the same IP but come from an un-recognized MAC.  This effectively blocks ARP spoofing or poisoning attacks and prevents unauthorized devices from hijacking an IP on your network.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control and MAC Filtering both let you use a device’s MAC address to decide whether it may join your LAN, but they operate at different scopes:

1. MAC Filtering  
   • Lives under the Wireless section of the router’s GUI.  
   • Only governs Wi-Fi clients.  
   • You turn it on, choose “Block wireless access” or “Allow wireless access only,” and then build a list of MAC addresses to block or permit.  

2. Access Control  
   • Lives under the Security (or Advanced → Security) section.  
   • Governs both wired and wireless clients.  
   • Lets you build a single Blacklist (devices that are never allowed) or Whitelist (devices that are the only ones allowed) for your entire network, regardless of how they’re connected.  

In short, if you need to police only your wireless network, MAC Filtering will do.  If you want one central allow/block list that applies to both Ethernet-connected and Wi-Fi-connected devices, use Access Control.

detailed_results.question: What are the possible causes if wireless devices cannot connect to the network?
detailed_results.expected: Possible causes include: WiFi is turned off on the router, incorrect wireless password entered, MAC Filtering blocking the device, incompatible wireless standard, or router needs to be restarted.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons a wireless client may fail to join a network:

1. Poor RF conditions  
   – The router’s signal is too weak (only 1–3 bars).  
   – Too much interference from nearby networks or devices (microwaves, cordless phones, etc.).  

2. Co-channel or adjacent-channel interference  
   – Your AP is using a crowded channel. Try switching it to 1, 6, or 11.  

3. Wireless adapter issues on the client  
   – The adapter’s driver is missing, outdated or corrupt.  
   – The client’s wireless radio is turned off (hardware switch or software “airplane” mode).  

4. OS/network utility conflicts (Windows)  
   – On XP, Wireless Zero Configuration (WZC) is disabled or a third-party utility (e.g. TP-LINK Utility) is managing the card.  
   – The WZC service isn’t running or is misconfigured.  

5. Authentication or encryption mismatches  
   – You’ve entered the wrong network key (case-sensitive).  
   – You’re confusing the router’s WPS PIN with its network security key.  
   – The encryption type set on the client (WEP/WPA/WPA2) doesn’t match the router’s.  

6. Miscellaneous  
   – DHCP not handing out an IP address (client stays at 169.254.x.x).  
   – MAC filtering or access‐control lists enabled on the router blocking the client’s MAC.  

Checking each of these points in turn will usually reveal why a device can’t join the WLAN.

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Bandwidth Control only works if every piece of the puzzle is set up exactly right.  In our experience the most common reasons it “doesn’t work” are:

1. You never enabled or saved the feature or individual rule  
   – On the Bandwidth Control page you must  
     • tick “Enable Bandwidth Control”  
     • enter your Total Up/Downstream bandwidth and click Save  
     • Add each rule, check “Enable this entry” and click OK  

2. The Total Up/Downstream values are wrong  
   – Don’t just type in the ISP’s advertised rate.  Do a quick speed-test and enter the real, tested Kbps values.  If you overstate the total, none of your per-PC limits will bite.

3. Wrong line type selected  
   – If you pick the wrong DSL line type (ATM vs. PTM, interleave vs. fast, etc.), the router can’t shape correctly.  When in doubt, call your ISP and ask what line profile you’re on.

4. IP-rule doesn’t match the device’s address  
   – If the PC’s IP is handed out by DHCP (and can change) your rule simply never sees that host.  Always either  
     • assign a static LAN IP on the PC, or  
     • reserve its address in the router’s DHCP table.

5. Overlapping or conflicting rules / wrong priorities  
   – Bandwidth Control applies the rule with the highest priority (numerically lowest “priority value”).  Make sure your IP ranges don’t overlap and that you haven’t accidentally given two rules the same priority number.

Once you’ve fixed any of the above, reboot the router just to be sure—and your per-PC upstream/downstream caps should start taking effect.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?

detailed_results.generated: The IP & MAC Binding feature (sometimes called ARP Binding) lets you lock a given IP address to a specific MAC address.  By doing so, the router will refuse any ARP traffic that claims that IP but comes from a different MAC, effectively stopping ARP-spoofing and related man-in-the-middle attacks on your LAN.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control is a more general device-level allow/deny feature for your whole LAN (both wired and wireless).  You maintain two lists—a whitelist of devices that are explicitly allowed onto the network and a blacklist of devices that are explicitly blocked.  The router checks every client’s MAC address against those lists and either admits or drops its traffic.

MAC Filtering, by contrast, is a simpler, wireless-only mechanism that lets you build a single “allowed” list of MAC addresses and then refuse association to any other wireless client.  

In practice the two differ mainly in scope and flexibility:  
• MAC Filtering  
  – Wireless only  
  – Whitelist-only: you list the MACs that may connect; all others are denied  
• Access Control  
  – Wired or wireless  
  – Both whitelist and blacklist supported: you can choose to block a few offenders or allow only a few trusted clients (or do both)

detailed_results.question: What are the possible causes if wireless devices cannot connect to the network?
detailed_results.expected: Possible causes include: WiFi is turned off on the router, incorrect wireless password entered, MAC Filtering blocking the device, incompatible wireless standard, or router needs to be restarted.

Possible causes fall into two broad categories:  
1. You can’t even see the network (“no SSID”)  
2. You can see the SSID but can’t join it  

Below is a consolidated list of common causes:

1. Wireless radio disabled  
   • On the router/modem: the WLAN/Wi-Fi LED is off or the wireless function has been turned off in its settings.  
   • On a laptop: the physical Wi-Fi switch (or Fn-key combo) is turned off.  

2. Adapter or driver issues  
   • The wireless adapter driver isn’t installed or has failed.  
   • The adapter is disabled in your operating system’s network settings.  

3. Out of range or poor signal  
   • You’re too far from the router—signal strength is weak (1–3 bars).  
   • Physical obstructions or radio interference reducing range.  

4. Incorrect SSID or region settings  
   • You are trying to join the wrong network name (SSID).  
   • The SSID is hidden (broadcast disabled) on the router.  
   • The router’s Region/Country setting doesn’t match your locale.  

5. Authentication/security mismatch  
   • You’re entering the wrong wireless password (Network Security Key)—it’s case-sensitive.  
   • You attempted WPS PIN but used the device PIN instead of the router’s PIN.  
   • The router is set to WPA/WPA2 or other mode that your device does not support.  

6. Windows-specific configuration blocks  
   • On Windows 7 “No connections are available” often means the radio is disabled.  
   • On Windows XP “Windows cannot configure this wireless connection” indicates XP is not managing the adapter—check vendor utilities.  
   • If you see errors like “Cannot join this network” or “Taking longer than usual,” troubleshoot signal strength and security settings.  

If you’ve checked all of the above and still cannot connect, try the built-in “Troubleshoot” utility (Windows) or reboot both your client device and your router.

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Bandwidth Control only works when the router can actually “see” and match the traffic you’ve told it to throttle – if you mis‐configure anything, or if your real line speed and your rule settings don’t line up, it simply won’t behave as you expect.  Common gotchas are:

1. You didn’t give your PCs the IPs (or IP ranges) you used in the rules  
   – if your machines pull dynamic (DHCP) addresses outside the range, the router never matches their traffic.

2. You forgot to cover the ports or protocols your applications actually use  
   – e.g. by leaving the default port range at 1–65535 you normally catch everything, but if an app uses non-TCP/UDP tunnels or encrypted VPNs it may slip under the radar.

3. The sum of all your “Upstream/Downstream” settings exceeds your real ISP bandwidth  
   – if you tell the router to allow 10 Mbps upstream on A and 10 Mbps on B but your ISP only gives you 8 Mbps, it can’t shape above the line rate, so the limits won’t hold.

4. Your modem/router is in bridge mode and the PPPoE (or PPTP/L2TP) dial is done by a PC  
   – the router never sees public-IP traffic to police, only bridged Ethernet frames, so it can’t rate-limit your Internet sessions.

5. You left Priority values at the default or gave everything the same priority  
   – if two devices both have “priority 5,” the router has no basis to favour one over the other, so “guaranteed minimum” or “maximum cap” rules may not be enforced as you intended.

6. Firmware bugs or model limitations  
   – very old or entry-level routers sometimes have half-baked QoS implementations.  If you suspect that, check for an updated firmware or the manufacturer’s notes on maximum shaping rates.

In practice, always make sure:  
• Each controlled device has a fixed IP that matches one of your rules.  
• Your upstream/downstream values in the router are set at or slightly below your true line speeds.  
• Your rules’ IP ranges, port ranges and protocols actually cover the traffic you want to limit.  
• Priority values are used to give strict guarantees or caps.  
• The router is terminating the Internet connection (not just bridged) so it can see and throttle all WAN traffic.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?

Once enabled, the router will only allow a device whose MAC matches the bound entry to use that IP.  This prevents ARP spoofing/poisoning and related attacks by blocking any host that claims your IP but doesn’t present the correct MAC.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control is a broader permitting/blocking mechanism for both wired and wireless clients.  Specifically, it lets you build  
 •  a whitelist (allowed devices) and  
 •  a blacklist (blocked devices)  

and then apply those lists to every device on your LAN, whether it’s connected over Ethernet or Wi-Fi.

By contrast, MAC Filtering is a simpler, wireless-only feature that uses only MAC addresses (and typically only an allow list) to decide which Wi-Fi clients may associate with your router.  

In short:  
 •  MAC Filtering = wireless only, MAC-address based allow list  
 •  Access Control = wired & wireless, MAC- and/or IP-based allow and block lists

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons you’ll see “Bandwidth Control” rules not actually throttling traffic the way you expect:

1. You entered the wrong total upload/download values  
   – If the “Total Upstream/Downstream Bandwidth” fields don’t exactly match what your ISP hands you (in Kbps), the router can’t calculate each client’s share properly.  Always convert Mbps→Kbps (1 Mbps = 1024 Kbps) and be sure to subtract any PPPoE or protocol‐overhead if your ISP requires it.

2. You chose the wrong “line type”  
   – TP-Link gives you several options (ADSL, Ethernet WAN, etc.).  If you pick the wrong one your router never actually measures or shapes the real traffic.  When in doubt, call your ISP and confirm which line type to select.

3. Your clients aren’t on fixed IPs  
   – Bandwidth rules are applied by IP address (or IP range).  If you’re using DHCP without address reservation, a computer’s IP can change and no rule will match.  Either give each machine a static IP or use the router’s “Address Reservation” feature.

4. There’s another NAT/router upstream  
   – If your TP-Link is sitting behind another modem/router that’s also doing NAT, the TP-Link never sees the true public‐side traffic.  Bandwidth control only works when the TP-Link is the one and only gateway.

5. Your rules overlap or exceed the total you set  
   – Make sure that the sum of all “minimum” and “maximum” allocations never exceeds your real total bandwidth.  Over‐allocating will produce unpredictable results.

6. Certain protocols or VPNs bypass port‐based shaping  
   – Encrypted tunnels, VPNs or P2P apps may use ports outside your defined ranges, so they slip past your TCP/UDP rules.  To catch those you’d need either a more advanced QoS engine or to open the port ranges wide enough to cover them.

If you check each of the above—correct total bandwidth, proper line type, fixed/​reserved IPs, single layer of NAT and non‐overlapping rules—your Bandwidth Control feature should start working as advertised.

By doing so, any device that tries to spoof the IP with a different MAC will be denied access.  In practice this prevents ARP spoofing and other ARP-based attacks on your LAN.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control is a feature that lets you explicitly block or allow any client device—whether it’s on Wi-Fi or plugged in by Ethernet—from using your network by maintaining either a blacklist (blocked devices) or a whitelist (allowed devices).  

MAC Filtering, by contrast, is strictly a wireless-only mechanism that simply uses each device’s unique MAC address to decide if it can join the Wi-Fi.  

Key differences:  
• Scope  
  – MAC Filtering applies only to wireless clients.  
  – Access Control applies to both wired and wireless clients.  

• Policy model  
  – MAC Filtering is usually set up as a single list of “permitted” or “denied” MAC addresses on the Wi-Fi.  
  – Access Control lets you choose between a blacklist (deny-list) or a whitelist (allow-list) for all network ports.
