   • Click “Add a New Keyword” (up to 200 entries each)  
   • To only allow access to specific sites, add them to the Whitelist (e.g. www.tp-link.com, wikipedia.org or just “wikipedia”)  
   • To block sites, add their domains or keywords to the Blacklist  
   • Click Save  

Once complete, the selected device will only be able to go online during your specified times and only visit sites you’ve whitelisted (if you set one).

detailed_results.question: How do you customize the USB disk server name?
detailed_results.expected: Log in to router, go to Advanced > USB Settings > Sharing Access, ensure Network Neighborhood is ticked, enter a custom Network/Media Server Name (e.g., MyShare), then click Save.
detailed_results.generated:
1. Open a browser and go to http://tplinkmodem.net  
2. Log in with your modem-router’s admin password.  
3. Navigate to Advanced → USB Settings → Sharing Access.  
4. Make sure “Network Neighborhood” (or “Enable NetBIOS”) is checked.  
5. In the “Network/Media Server Name” field enter the name you want (for example, MyShare).  
6. Click Save.  

After a few seconds the USB disk will be visible on your network under the new server name.

detailed_results.question: How do you enable MAC Filtering to control wireless access?
detailed_results.expected: Go to Advanced > Wireless > MAC Filtering in the router interface, enable the function, then add MAC addresses to either allow or block specific devices from accessing the wireless network.
detailed_results.generated:
To turn on MAC‐based filtering for your Wi-Fi clients, do the following:

1. In a web browser go to http://tplinkmodem.net and log in with your router password.  
2. From the menu navigate to Advanced → Wireless → MAC Filtering.  
3. Check “Enable Wireless MAC Filtering.”  
4. Under “Filtering Rule” pick one of:  
   • Block wireless access from the devices in the list below  (Blacklist)  
   • Allow wireless access only from the devices in the list below (Whitelist)  
5. Click Save.  

If you chose “Block”  
  a. In the Devices Online table, check the box next to each device you wish to block.  
  b. Click the “Block” button above that table.  

If you chose “Allow”  
  a. Click Add.  
  b. Paste or type the client’s MAC Address and give it a name/description.  
  c. Check “Enable this entry,” then click OK.  

Once you Save your settings, only the MAC addresses on your approved list (or conversely, all but those on your block list) will be able to associate to your wireless network.

detailed_results.question: What should you do if you cannot access the router's web interface?
detailed_results.expected: Check that your device is connected to the router (wired or wireless), verify you're using the correct address (tplinkmodem.net or 192.168.1.1), try a different web browser, and ensure no firewall is blocking access.
detailed_results.generated:
First, make sure it isn’t just a bad cable or PC‐side IP setting:

1. Check that the Ethernet cable between your PC and the router is firmly plugged in (and that the router is powered on).  
2. Verify your PC’s network settings – if you’ve been given a static IP by your ISP or by your IT department, make sure it’s set correctly; otherwise set your PC to “Obtain an IP address automatically.”

If you still cannot reach http://tplinkmodem.net (or the router’s LAN IP):

3. Restore the router to factory defaults using the RESET button on the back:  
   • With the router powered on, press and hold the WPS/RESET button for about 8 seconds.  
   • Wait for all LEDs to flash, then release.  
   • The router will reboot with its default LAN IP and login credentials.  

4. Once it comes back up, point your browser to http://tplinkmodem.net (or 192.168.1.1), log in with the default admin password, and run the Quick Setup Wizard to re-configure it.

If after all of that you still can’t log in, contact TP-Link Technical Support.

detailed_results.question: How do you recover access if you forgot the router's login password?
detailed_results.expected: If you forgot the password, you must reset the router to factory defaults by pressing and holding the RESET button for 8 seconds. After reset, you'll need to set a new password when accessing the router.
detailed_results.generated:
If you’ve lost the admin (web-management) password, the only way to regain access is to reset the modem-router back to factory defaults.  Here’s how:

1.  With the router powered on, press and hold the WPS/RESET button on the back for about 8 seconds (until all the LEDs flash).  
2.  Release the button and wait for the router to reboot.  
3.  Once it’s back up, the web-management password will have reverted to the factory default (often blank or “admin” – check your product label or quick-install guide).  
4.  Log in at http://tplinkmodem.net (or its default IP), go to System Tools > Backup & Restore, and click “Factory Restore” if needed.  
5.  As soon as you regain access, go to System Tools > Administration (or similar) and set a new admin password (1–15 characters).  

Note:  Resetting erases all of your current settings, so you’ll have to re-configure your WAN, LAN, wireless SSID/password, port forwards, etc., unless you previously saved a configuration backup.

detailed_results.question: What does it mean if the ADSL LED is not lit on the router?
detailed_results.expected: If the ADSL LED is not lit, it means there's no DSL connection. Check that the DSL cable is properly connected to the phone jack or splitter, verify the cable is not damaged, and confirm DSL service is active with your ISP.
detailed_results.generated:
If the ADSL LED is off (not lit), it means the modem/router has failed to synchronize with your DSL line. In other words, there is no active ADSL link.  

Suggested steps:  
1. Check that your phone line and ADSL filter are properly connected (see “Connect Your Modem/Router” in your manual).  
2. Make sure the cables aren’t damaged and the filter is correctly installed on every phone jack.  
3. If your setup is correct and the LED is still off, contact your ISP to verify that your ADSL service is up and running.

detailed_results.question: What are the possible causes if wireless devices cannot connect to the network?
detailed_results.expected: Possible causes include: WiFi is turned off on the router, incorrect wireless password entered, MAC Filtering blocking the device, incompatible wireless standard, or router needs to be restarted.
detailed_results.generated:
Possible causes fall into three broad categories—authentication, signal/interference, and adapter/configuration problems:

1. Authentication problems  
  • Incorrect wireless password (network security key) or PIN (case-sensitive)  
  • Using the router’s setup PIN instead of the actual WPA/WPA2 key  
  • Mismatch between your chosen security type (WEP/WPA/WPA2) and the router’s settings  

2. Poor signal or RF interference  
  • Too weak a signal (1–3 bars)—move closer to the router or remove obstacles  
  • Neighboring networks crowding the same channel—switch your router’s channel to 1, 6, or 11 to reduce overlap  

3. Wireless-adapter or driver issues  
  • Wireless radio disabled (hardware switch or Fn key turned off on laptops)  
  • Adapter disabled in Windows’ Network Connections or BIOS/UEFI  
  • Missing, corrupt, or outdated wireless-adapter driver—reinstall or update the driver  

4. Operating-system or utility conflicts  
  • On Windows 7: wireless may be “blocked” (No connections are available)—use the built-in Troubleshooter or enable the radio  
  • On Windows XP: if “Windows cannot configure this wireless connection,” a third-party utility may be controlling the adapter—disable one of them so only one config tool runs  

If you check each of these areas—credentials, signal/interference, adapter status/driver, and OS-level configuration—you’ll usually identify why a device won’t join the network.

detailed_results.question: Why might bandwidth control not work as expected?
detailed_results.expected: Bandwidth control requires proper configuration of bandwidth rules for each device or IP range. Ensure you've set up rules correctly, assigned appropriate bandwidth limits, and that devices are properly identified in the system.
detailed_results.generated:
Here are the most common reasons people find that “Bandwidth Control” simply doesn’t take effect on their TP-Link (or similar) home routers:

1. You never enabled it or set the global line-speed  
   • On TP-Link you must first go into Bandwidth Control → Settings, check “Enable,” and enter your actual Upstream and Downstream line rates (what your ISP actually hands you).   If you skip that step and go straight to adding rules, the router has no idea how fast your WAN link is, so it won’t police anything.  

2. Your rules aren’t matching the traffic  
   • IP Range wrong – if your PCs are getting dynamic DHCP addresses that drift around, the “IP Range” in your rule won’t match, so none of their packets get shaped.  Either make the PCs’ LAN addresses static or reserve them in DHCP.  
   • Port/Protocol mismatch – by default TP-Link’s port-range is 1–65535 and protocol is “ALL,” but if you change those and then generate traffic on an un-covered port or protocol (e.g. you pick TCP only, but the application uses UDP), the rule won’t catch it.  

3. You exceeded or mis-allocated your total  
   • If the sum of all your per-host max-rates exceeds the global total you entered, the router can’t enforce your caps cleanly.  
   • Likewise if you give someone a super-low priority value (e.g. “1” on TP-Link) they’ll always jump to the head of the queue and can starve everyone else.  

4. Shaping download is inherently “fuzzy”  
   • Upload-rate control is precise (you drop or delay your own packets).  Downstream policing relies on delaying or dropping ACKs, so it can never be quite as tight, and you may still see short bursts above your cap.  

5. You’re watching purely LAN (peer-to-peer) traffic  
   • Bandwidth Control only governs traffic going in and out of the WAN port.  If two PCs talk over the LAN side, the router won’t touch it.  

Checklist to get it working:  
  a) In the global Bandwidth Control settings, enable the feature and enter your ISP’s true up/down speeds.  
  b) Assign (or reserve) fixed IPs for every client you want to shape.  
  c) Create one rule per IP (or IP-range), leave port range at 1–65535, protocol = ALL, set appropriate priority/guaranteed/max up & down, and make sure the rule is “enabled.”  
  d) Double-check that the sum of all “Max” values doesn’t exceed your global total.  
  e) Save and reboot if you still see no change.  

If you follow all of the above and it still “doesn’t work,” it’s possible your firmware is buggy—or simply that your ISP link is so variable (for example on some ADSL lines) that shaping your download looks ineffective. But in almost every case the culprit is one of the five points above.

detailed_results.question: What is the purpose of IP & MAC Binding feature?
detailed_results.expected: IP & MAC Binding (ARP) prevents ARP spoofing and ARP attacks by binding specific IP addresses to specific MAC addresses, ensuring only authorized devices can use those IP addresses on the network.
detailed_results.generated:
The IP & MAC Binding feature (sometimes called ARP Binding) exists to hard‐link each device’s IP address to its unique MAC address.  By doing so, the router will:

1. Refuse any ARP reply that claims a bound IP but comes from a different MAC  
2. Block “rogue” devices that try to hijack an IP through ARP spoofing or impersonation  
3. Let you effectively whitelist (or blacklist) specific clients by IP/MAC pair, without having to change your Wi-Fi password every time

In short, IP & MAC Binding prevents ARP-based attacks and stops unauthorized devices from joining your network by ensuring only the exact MAC you’ve registered can use each IP.

detailed_results.question: What is Access Control and how does it differ from MAC Filtering?
detailed_results.expected: Access Control allows blocking or allowing specific devices for both wired and wireless networks, while MAC Filtering works only for wireless network access. Access Control uses blacklist or whitelist approach.
detailed_results.generated:
Access Control is the umbrella feature in your router that lets you build “allow” (whitelist) or “deny” (blacklist) policies for any device—wired or wireless—based on its identity (MAC address and, in some implementations, IP address).  You turn Access Control on in the Advanced → Security menu, choose whether you want to block listed devices or allow only listed devices, and then populate that list.

MAC Filtering, by contrast, is the specific mechanism used to protect *wireless* clients by their 12-digit MAC address.  In most home routers you’ll see MAC Filtering presented as an option under Access Control; it simply means “apply your allow/deny list only to Wi-Fi and only by MAC.”  

In short:
• Access Control = the general feature (black/white lists, wired & wireless, MAC and sometimes IP)  
• MAC Filtering = the wireless-only, MAC-address-only implementation of that feature

detailed_results.question: How can you remotely access USB storage connected to the router?
detailed_results.expected: Enable the FTP Server feature in USB Settings. You can then access your USB disk remotely via FTP outside your local network, useful for sharing large files without cloud services.
detailed_results.generated:
Most TP-Link modem-routers let you share a USB drive over the Internet by running a built-in FTP server.  In a nutshell the steps are:  
1.  Plug your USB disk into the router’s USB port and wait for the USB LED to go solid.  
2.  Log in to the router’s web interface and go to Advanced → USB Settings → FTP Server.  
3.  Enable the FTP Server and, if required, create a username/password (you can often leave the default “anonymous” account enabled or add a specific user for better security).  
4.  Note the WAN (Internet-side) IP address or DDNS host name of your router and the FTP port (default is 21).  
5.  From anywhere on the Internet open an FTP client (or even a browser) and point it at:  
     ftp://<your-wan-ip>  
   or  
     ftp://<your-ddns-hostname>  
   – if you set a custom port, append “:port” to the address.  
6.  Log in with the account you configured and browse/upload/download files just as you would on your local network share.  

That’s all there is to it—your USB disk becomes an Internet-accessible FTP server.
